title: Hide Artifacts: Run Virtual Instance
summary: Run Virtual Instance covers adversaries executing their tooling inside a virtual machine, emulator or sandbox on an already compromised host, so that host-based sensors observe only the virtualisation process. Native hypervisors, lightweight emulators and portable hypervisor binaries all serve this purpose, and temporary sandboxes defined by small configuration files are especially quick to stand up. Shared folders and mapped drives then give the guest a path back into the host file system. Traffic from the guest can appear under a different address or host name, which frustrates attribution. Detection rests on hypervisor process and image-file telemetry, new virtual network adapters, and guest-to-host sharing events, weighed against sanctioned virtualisation and malware analysis use.

beginner.definition: A virtual instance is a computer that runs inside another computer. It has its own pretend hardware, disk and network. Attackers can run their tools inside it, so the real machine mostly shows a virtual machine program. This makes their activity harder to see and harder to trace.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security tools on the real machine often cannot see inside a virtual instance. The attacker's files and commands stay inside a separate disk image. Traffic from the virtual machine can also look like it comes from a different computer. Incident responders may waste time chasing the wrong address. Spotting virtualisation that nobody asked for is therefore valuable.
howItWorks: The attacker installs or reuses virtualisation software, such as the built in Windows hypervisor, on the victim machine.
They start a virtual machine and load their tools inside its own operating system.
Some tools are lightweight emulators that need only a few files copied onto the host.
A shared folder or mapped drive can connect the virtual machine back to the host files.
Traffic leaving the virtual machine may carry a different address or host name than the host.
Temporary sandboxes can be defined by a small configuration file that maps folders and runs a command.
beginner.example: Imagine a house with a strict guard at the front door. The guard checks everyone who walks in and writes down their name. One tenant parks a caravan in the garden and lives in it instead. The guard never sees the tenant enter, because the caravan has its own small door. The tenant still uses the house water and power, and sometimes passes notes through a hatch. A virtual instance is that caravan. The activity is real and it touches the house, but the front door log says nothing.
takeaways: A virtual machine on a workstation can hide activity from tools on the host.
New virtual network adapters and large image files are useful warning signs.
Shared folders between a guest and its host deserve a close look.

objectives: Define a virtual instance and explain why it hides activity from host tools.
List the ways an attacker can obtain virtualisation on a compromised host.
Explain how shared folders connect a guest system back to the host.
Identify telemetry for hypervisor processes, network adapters and image files.
Separate sanctioned virtualisation from an attacker controlled instance.
